questions.question: Why is a watermark alone not enough to secure a voice generation system?
options: Because watermarks make audio too loud
Because attackers may generate or modify audio without preserving the watermark
Because watermarks can only be used on text files
Because watermarks replace the need for consent checks
questions.explanation: A watermark helps identify compliant, cooperative outputs, but it does not stop adversaries from generating unmarked audio or stripping the mark through transformations. That is why the lesson pairs watermarking with anti-spoof detection.

questions.question: What does Equal Error Rate (EER) measure in detection tasks?
options: The sample rate where both clips match
The point where false accepts and false rejects are equal
The number of watermark bits recovered
The latency of the detector in milliseconds
questions.explanation: EER is a threshold-based metric that summarizes the tradeoff between accepting spoofs and rejecting genuine audio. It is commonly used in speaker verification and anti-spoofing benchmarks because it gives one operating-point summary.

questions.question: What three defense layers does the lesson recommend for 2026 voice systems?
options: Compression, normalization, and denoising
Anti-spoof detection, audio watermarking, and authenticated provenance
Only liveness prompts and speaker embeddings
Only encryption and GPU attestation
questions.explanation: The lesson organizes defenses into three related layers: a detector for real-vs-fake classification, a watermark for AI-generated outputs, and signed provenance metadata like C2PA. The point is that no single layer covers all attack surfaces.

questions.question: What is one major advantage of AudioSeal highlighted in the lesson?
options: It stores unlimited payload bits with no distortion
It is localized, fast, and robust to common edits like compression and noise
It is the best defense against aggressive pitch shifting
It removes the need for any detector
questions.explanation: The lesson presents AudioSeal as the default open watermark because it can detect marks at fine temporal resolution, runs very fast, and survives common transformations such as MP3 or AAC compression and modest speed or noise changes. Those properties make it practical for production workflows.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what attack is the universal weakness for current audio watermarks?
options: Silence trimming
Pitch shifting
File renaming
Stereo-to-mono conversion
questions.explanation: The lesson quotes benchmark evidence that pitch shift can collapse bit recovery accuracy across watermark methods. That weakness is exactly why the system should not rely on watermarking alone and must also deploy anti-spoof detectors.
